us-house.budget-law-health: a budget law under which national funding of public health coverage for low-income residents falls by about 14 percent across ten years and that coverage becomes subject to work requirements. According to the official estimate, about 3 percent of residents lose their health coverage as a consequence
us-house.subsidy-extension: extending for three years the expanded premium subsidies for health insurance that people buy individually. That insurance covers about 7 percent of residents, and by an independent estimate subsidized buyers' average premium payment would more than double without the extension
us-house.employer-plan-bill: a bill relaxing the rules that apply to health plans run by employers and associations and financing payments that reduce cost sharing in individual insurance. By the official estimate, premiums for individual insurance before subsidies would fall by about 11 percent and the number of residents with coverage would fall by about 0.03 percent
us-house.budget-law-food: the same budget law, under which national funding of food assistance for low-income households also falls by about 16 percent across ten years

uk-commons.benefit-law: a law under which the standard rate of the main benefit for working-age people rises faster than inflation for four years, a change the government estimated would raise income for about one in seven households, and under which new applicants receive a health-related supplement to that benefit about half as large, while current recipients and people with the most severe lifelong conditions are not affected
uk-commons.child-limit-removal: a law abolishing the rule under which a family received child-related benefit payments only for its first two children. By the government's estimate, about one in ten children is affected by the change and about 3 percent of all children are lifted out of poverty

de-bundestag.health-savings-law: a savings law for health insurance that, to keep contribution rates stable, increased what patients pay for medicines by half, narrowed the free coverage of spouses in public health insurance, and limited increases in payments to doctors, hospitals, and drug makers
de-bundestag.pension-law: a pension law under which the public pension stays at 48 percent of average wages until the end of 2031 and parents whose children were born before 1992 gain six months of pension entitlement for each child
de-bundestag.basic-income-reform: a reform putting a stricter scheme in place of the main basic income benefit, which goes to about 7 percent of residents. Benefit rates are unchanged; refusing training brings a 30 percent cut in benefits for three months, a second missed appointment brings a cut for one month, and further missed appointments can lead to the benefit being withdrawn in full

ca-commons.annual-budget-health: the annual budget, under which the public dental plan, public drug coverage, and subsidized child care carry on with no new funding added for them
ca-commons.annual-budget-meals: the same annual budget, under which a national school meals program also becomes permanent, reaching up to 400,000 more children a year, about 1 percent of residents

fr-assemblee.retirement-age-suspension: a pause in a law that was raising the retirement age, under which that age stays at 62 years and 9 months until 2028, so that people born from 1964 to 1968, about 5 percent of residents, can retire three to six months sooner
fr-assemblee.social-insurance-budget: the annual social insurance budget, under which that pause took effect and a planned freeze on pensions and minimum benefits was abandoned, so that they rose about 0.9 percent with prices
fr-assemblee.social-insurance-budget-health: the same annual social insurance budget, under which the national target for public health spending rose by about 3 percent from the previous year
fr-assemblee.negotiated-exit-benefits: a law under which people who leave a job by mutual agreement can draw unemployment benefits for a shorter maximum period, from 18 down to 15 months for those under 55 and up to about a quarter less for older workers. Such exits make up over a quarter of unemployment benefit spending, and the government put the saving at up to about 3 percent of that spending
